rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.
The answer explicitly provides the substance of the requirement by stating that Annex IV point 1(e) requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is not "medium risk": the AI Act has no medium-risk tier, and this system is high-risk under Article 6(1). Both conditions of Article 6(1) are met, whatever class the device has under the MDR: (a) the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, here Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (Annex I, point 11); and (b) that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. This applies even if the AI system is placed on the market separately from the device. The Article 6(3) derogation cannot apply because it covers only Annex III systems, and under Article 43(3) the AI requirements are assessed within the MDR notified-body procedure.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the AI Act has no medium-risk tier and correctly identifies the system as high-risk.
The answer states that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, specifically citing Regulation (EU) 2017/745.
The answer confirms that the product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under the applicable legislation.
The answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative and apply regardless of the device's sectoral risk classification.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and under Annex III it is not high-risk. Why it is not prohibited: Article 5(1) prohibits biometric categorisation that infers sensitive attributes (point (g)). It also prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement (point (h)). One-to-one verification is neither of these. Why it is not high-risk under Annex III: Article 6(2) makes Annex III systems high-risk, but Annex III point 1(a) excludes "AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be." The exclusion only holds if verification really is the sole purpose. The system would come back into Annex III if it also performed biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes (point 1(b)) or emotion recognition (point 1(c)). One exception to check: under Article 6(1), the system would still be high-risk if it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, or is itself such a product, and that product needs a third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states the system is not prohibited and explains that one-to-one biometric verification does not fall under the prohibited practices in Article 5(1)(g) or (h), thereby conveying the substance that such a system is not prohibited.

The answer states the system is not high-risk under Annex III due to the exclusion in Annex III.1(a), and correctly notes the conditionality of that exclusion, thus conveying the substance that it is not high-risk unless other factors apply.
The answer explicitly references and applies the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification with the sole purpose of confirming identity, stating it directly and explaining its scope.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with clear structure and logical flow; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in coherent, actionable prose.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 governs human oversight, requiring that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while they are in use (Article 14(1)). Oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and they may be built into the system by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement (Article 14(3)). Overseers must be enabled to understand the system's capacities and limitations and monitor its operation, stay aware of automation bias, correctly interpret its output, and disregard, override or reverse that output, or intervene or halt the system with a "stop" button or similar procedure (Article 14(4)).
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that Article 14 governs human oversight.
The answer cites Article 14(1), stating that systems must be designed so natural persons can effectively oversee them during use.
The answer references the purpose of oversight in preventing or minimizing risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, aligning with Article 14(2).
The answer describes oversight measures as either built in by the provider or identified by the provider for deployer implementation, matching Article 14(3).
The answer lists all key capabilities required for overseers: understanding, monitoring, interpreting, overriding, and halting the system, as specified in Article 14(4).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in clear prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly acknowledges the existence of exceptions under Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly excludes (c) and (d) from the exception.
The answer states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance audience.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Under Article 99(3), breaching the Article 5 prohibited AI practices can lead to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. This is the highest fine ceiling in the Regulation, above the EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % ceiling in Article 99(4), which expressly excludes Article 5. For SMEs, including start-ups, Article 99(6) applies the lower of the two amounts, either the percentage or the fixed amount.
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the fine amount as EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, matching the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fines to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, uses neutral and professional language consistent with regulatory definitions, and presents the information in a single, clear sentence suitable for a compliance context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I and Annex III, capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems are subject to Article 50 transparency duties, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer acknowledges minimal or no risk systems are not subject to high-risk obligations and notes the availability of voluntary codes under Article 95, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming that a non-provider operator can be seen as a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service triggers provider status.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering action.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk AI system (including general-purpose) so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 1(1), the objective of the EU AI Act is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI. It must also ensure a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems while supporting innovation.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of improving the functioning of the internal market.
The answer states the substance of promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer states the full scope of protection, including health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI systems.
The answer explicitly mentions supporting innovation as part of the objective.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, clearly aligning with the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and that it falls under Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer includes the condition that the derogation does not apply if the system profiles natural persons, stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which conveys the required exception.

The answer references Article 6(4) and states that the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, satisfying the requirement to state the substance of the obligation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5), the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on providers of general-purpose AI models. When it reviews such a decision, the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine. This covers fines the Commission imposes under Article 101(1), which can reach 3% of annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher.
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine,' which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel the fine,' matching the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the Court 'may reduce the fine,' which matches criterion 3.
The answer states the Court 'may increase the fine,' conveying the substance of criterion 4.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Under Article 49(1) and Article 71(2), the provider or authorised representative of an Annex III high-risk system must enter the Section A information of Annex VIII (point 2 systems are instead registered at national level under Article 49(5)). The required items are: the provider's name, address and contact details; the same details for any person submitting on its behalf; the authorised representative's details, where applicable; the trade name and a traceability reference; the intended purpose, components and functions; a basic description of the data, inputs and operating logic; the system's status; the notified-body certificate's type, number and expiry date and that body's name or identification number, where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate; the Member States concerned; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use; and an optional URL. For Annex III points 1, 6 and 7 systems in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, Article 49(4) requires registration in a secure non-public section, limited to Section A points 1 to 5, 7 and 10. And excludes points 6, 8 and 9, Section B points 6 to 7 and 10 to 11, and Section C.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer lists the provider's contact details, those of any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable, satisfying the substance of criterion 1.
The answer includes the trade name and a traceability reference, which matches the requirement in criterion 2.
The answer states that the provider must submit the intended purpose, components, and functions, which corresponds to the substance of criterion 3.
The answer refers to a 'basic description of the data, inputs and operating logic', capturing the substance of criterion 4.
The answer includes the system's status and the notified body certificate details (type, number, expiry, body name/ID) and a scanned copy where applicable, satisfying criterion 5.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: The answer states that processing is allowed only when strictly necessary for bias detection/correction and cannot be effectively achieved with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.
The answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security measures and pseudonymisation.
The answer describes strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and explicitly prohibits transmission, transfer, or access by other parties.
The answer states that the data must be deleted once bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.

The answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, and not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3), the provider's instructions for use must give deployers the following categories of information. They must include: (a) the identity and contact details of the provider and any authorised representative; (b) the system's characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations, meaning its intended purpose, level of accuracy (including metrics), robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15, known or foreseeable risk circumstances, capabilities to explain output, performance for specific persons or groups, input-data and training-data specifications, and information for interpreting output; and (c) changes predetermined at the initial conformity assessment. They must also cover (d) human oversight measures under Article 14; (e) needed computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance and care measures including software updates; and (f) mechanisms to collect, store and interpret logs under Article 12.

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant

The answer includes all listed sub-elements of characteristics, capabilities, and performance limitations, such as intended purpose, accuracy metrics, robustness, cybersecurity, foreseeable risks, explainability, performance for specific groups, and input/training data specifications.
The answer refers to changes predetermined at the initial conformity assessment.
The answer explicitly mentions human oversight measures under Article 14.
The answer includes computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance measures including software updates.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Under Article 95, codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both. Under Article 95(3), any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, may also be involved. Under Article 95(1), the AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of these codes, including related governance mechanisms, to foster voluntary application of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), providers of high-risk AI systems must keep a quality management system, documented in written policies, procedures and instructions. It must include at least. A regulatory-compliance strategy, including conformity assessment and managing modifications, techniques for design, design control and design verification, techniques for development, quality control and quality assurance, examination, test and validation procedures, and how often they are run, technical specifications, including standards, systems and procedures for data management, the risk management system, a post-market monitoring system under Article 72, procedures for reporting serious incidents, handling communication with authorities, notified bodies, other operators and customers, record-keeping systems, resource management, including security-of-supply measures, an accountability framework for management and staff. Under Article 17(2), how these are implemented can be proportionate to the provider's size. The required rigour and level of protection still apply.
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

The answer states 'systems and procedures for data management', covering the data lifecycle as required.
The answer explicitly includes 'the risk management system' and 'a post-market monitoring system under Article 72'.
The answer includes 'record-keeping systems' and 'an accountability framework for management and staff'.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Article 5(1)(h), law enforcement may use "real-time" remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces only where it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives: the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and the search for missing persons; the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or of a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist attack; and locating or identifying a person suspected of an Annex II offence punishable in the Member State concerned by a maximum custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. Under Article 5(2), any such use may only confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual. It also requires a completed Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment and registration under Article 49, which in urgent cases may be completed without undue delay after use begins.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Under Article 50(2), providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of different types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The obligation does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing, where it does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or its semantics, or where its use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.

Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: Under Article 88(1), the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models, taking into account the applicable procedural guarantees. The Commission entrusts the implementation of these tasks to the AI Office. This does not affect the Commission's powers of organisation or the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties. Under Article 88(2), national market surveillance authorities may ask the Commission to use these powers where this is necessary and proportionate to help them carry out their own tasks under the Regulation.

AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Under Article 60(4)(e), data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions may be transferred to a third country only if appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented. This is one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met before testing can take place. The Act does not define these safeguards itself. It points to existing Union law, mainly the GDPR's rules on international transfers, with extra protection where special categories of personal data under GDPR Article 9 are involved.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer, which matches the substance of the criterion.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions do not all have to be met. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the listed conditions, so either one is enough on its own. The first condition, in Article 51(1)(a), is that the model has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; Article 51(2) presumes this when the cumulative computation used to train it is greater than 10^25 floating point operations. The second condition, in Article 51(1)(b), is a Commission decision that the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to high-impact capabilities, having regard to the Annex XIII criteria; the Commission can take this decision on its own initiative or after a qualified alert from the scientific panel.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of condition (a), including the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs as specified in Article 51(2).
The answer clearly explains condition (b), including the Commission's role and reference to Annex XIII criteria, as well as the triggers for its decision.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No, it is not automatically high-risk. Under Article 6(1), an AI system is high-risk only if two conditions are both met: under point (a), it is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, which includes the MDR (Regulation (EU) 2017/745) at Annex I point 11; and under point (b), that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. A Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified by the manufacturer without a notified body, so condition (b) fails. Such a system is therefore high-risk only by the separate Article 6(2) route, which applies only if its intended purpose matches a use case listed in Annex III.
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1)(a) and (b) must be fulfilled, conveying their cumulative nature.

The answer concludes that because condition (b) fails, the system does not meet Article 6(1), correctly linking the failure of condition (b) to the inapplicability of the provision.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes, under Article 6(1), an AI system used as a safety component in a lift is high-risk if two cumulative conditions are met, whether or not it is placed on the market separately from the lift. Under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and point 4 of Annex I lists Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts. Under Article 6(1)(b), that product must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that Directive before it is placed on the market or put into service. The Article 6(3) derogation applies only to Annex III systems, so it does not apply here.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its opening word and maintains that position throughout.
The answer states the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and specifically cites Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts as listed in Annex I.
The answer states that the product must be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the applicable Directive before being placed on the market or put into service.
The answer explicitly describes the two conditions as 'cumulative' and uses the phrase 'two cumulative conditions are met'.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both duties apply, and neither waits for the market surveillance authority. Under Article 20(2), once the provider becomes aware of a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), it must immediately investigate the causes, together with the reporting deployer where applicable. It must then inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body of the nature of the non-compliance and any corrective action taken. Under Article 20(1), if the provider considers or has reason to consider the system non-conforming, it must immediately bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it, and inform distributors, deployers, authorised representatives and importers. The authority's own evaluation under Article 79(2) runs in parallel: operators must cooperate, and the authority may require corrective action within at most 15 working days. The operator must also ensure corrective action across all affected systems it has made available on the Union market (Article 79(4)); otherwise, the authority takes provisional measures (Article 79(5)).
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both duties apply.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's obligation to immediately bring the system into conformity or take corrective actions such as withdrawal or recall.
The answer clearly assigns the duty to investigate causes to the provider under Article 20(2), not to the market surveillance authority.
The answer specifies that investigation is done in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and does not defer to the market surveillance authority.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate: under Article 24(3), distributors must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements. The duty applies only "where applicable," so it matters mainly where the AI system is shipped or stored as physical hardware or as part of a product, and it may not apply to software delivered purely by download. If those conditions do compromise conformity, Article 24(4) requires the operator to take corrective action, withdraw or recall the system, or make sure the provider, importer or another relevant operator does so. And the authorities competent for the high-risk AI system concerned, giving details, in particular, of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken.

Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly confirms that the model did not hallucinate, affirming the correctness of the statement.
The answer cites and states the substance of Article 24(3), confirming its applicability.

The answer explains that the duty applies only 'where applicable,' clarifying that it pertains to physical shipment or storage, such as on hardware or physical media, and may not apply to purely digital delivery.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: No, the AI Act does not ban or classify drones as such; it classifies an AI system by its intended purpose, whatever device carries it. Using AI on a drone to identify people around town is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) when it is real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, except strictly for the searches, threats and suspects listed in Article 5(1)(h)(i), (iii). Any other remote biometric identification is high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III.1(a). Separately, biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation is prohibited under Article 5(1)(g). A toy drone falls under the Toy Safety Directive listed in Annex I.2, and a non-toy drone falls under the civil aviation regulation listed in Annex I.20. Under Article 6(1), the AI is high-risk only if it is a safety component of the drone, or the product itself, and that legislation requires a third-party conformity assessment. If a toy drone is used for another purpose, such as identifying people, that use is judged under Article 5 and Annex III in the same way as any other drone.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on intended purpose, not the device type, aligning with Article 6
Correctly identifies use of AI in drones for identifying people in public as remote biometric identification, falling under Annex III.1(a) and not the verification exclusion
Explains that toy status does not exempt the system from classification based on intended use
Clarifies that a toy drone used for other applications is assessed based on that use against Annex III or Article 6(1), consistent with the criteria

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: Yes, the operator can go ahead, and the Act does not require high-risk logs for that new use. This holds only if the operator's legal team is right that neither route applies. Article 6(1) makes a system high-risk as a safety component or product under Annex I legislation that requires third-party conformity assessment, and Article 6(2) makes a use high-risk if it matches an Annex III use case. If neither applies, the new use is not high-risk. Changing the intended purpose makes you a provider under Article 25(1)(c) only if the system becomes high-risk under Article 6. A substantial modification under Article 25(1)(b) counts only where the system remains high-risk. So neither shift of provider duties is triggered, and the Article 12 automatic-logging regime does not apply to this use. The operator's existing high-risk use keeps all its current obligations. If the new use turns out to fit an Annex III use case, or involves profiling people, the Article 6(3) exemption would not help you, and the operator's conclusion would change.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use

The candidate answer does not state that Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use, nor does it explain that deviating from intended use violates this obligation regardless of risk classification. rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, it is potentially high-risk under Article 6(1) with Annex I, point 11 (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices), not under Annex III. Article 6(1) makes it high-risk when both conditions are met: (a) the AI system is a medical device, or a safety component of one, covered by the MDR; and (b) that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment. In practice, MDR Rule 11 usually puts software that informs therapeutic decisions in class IIa or higher, which requires a notified body. Annex III does not list clinical treatment support as such; its healthcare items cover only public-authority eligibility for healthcare services (point 5(a)) and emergency patient triage (point 5(d)).
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

The answer attributes the high-risk classification to Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and therefore does not state the substance of the criterion.

rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured explanation using precise regulatory references without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four items and no to the last: the operator must disclose the date of release, the number of parameters, how the model interacts with hardware (where applicable) and the licence, but not samples of outlier data. This comes from Article 53(1)(b)(ii), which requires GPAI providers to give providers integrating the model at least the elements in Annex XII. Those elements are the date of release and methods of distribution (Annex XII.1(c)), the architecture and number of parameters (Annex XII.1(f)), how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable (Annex XII.1(d)), and the licence for the model (Annex XII.1(h)). For training data, Annex XII.2(c) only requires information on the type and provenance of the data and on curation methodologies, where applicable, so no samples of outlier data are required. Under Article 53(1)(b), this information is provided without prejudice to protecting intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets. Under Article 53(2), the duty does not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, unless the model has systemic risk.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, healthcare decision-making as such is not one of the eight high-risk areas in Annex III. Under Article 6(2), those areas are biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Healthcare systems are high-risk under Article 6(2) only if they fit a listed use case: public-authority eligibility decisions for essential benefits including healthcare services (Annex III, point 5(a)), life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing (point 5(c)), or emergency healthcare patient triage (point 5(d)). The Article 6(3) exemption can apply, but never where the system profiles people. Separately, under Article 6(1) and Annex I, AI that is a medical or in vitro diagnostic device, or a safety component of one, is high-risk if the device needs third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No

The answer clearly states that healthcare decision-making as such is not one of the listed high-risk areas, which matches the 'No' verdict required by the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents regulatory distinctions precisely.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Guardrails do not move an agentic system from high-risk to "moderate" risk, because the Act has no moderate-risk tier. High-risk status comes from the system's intended purpose falling within a use-case listed in Annex III, not from how well its risks are controlled. Guardrails are risk-control measures that a high-risk provider must adopt under the Article 9 risk-management system. Any residual risk must still be judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer (Article 9(6)). The system therefore stays high-risk and keeps all its Article 8 obligations. Only the Commission can remove a use-case from Annex III, by delegated act under Article 7(3). It can do so only where the use-case no longer poses significant risks and removing it does not lower overall protection. Changing the intended purpose can change the classification. If the purpose is narrowed so it no longer matches an Annex III use-case, the system falls outside the high-risk regime. Changes can also shift obligations. Anyone who modifies the purpose so that the system becomes high-risk is treated as its provider (Article 25(1)(c)). Anyone who substantially modifies a system that remains high-risk is also treated as its provider (Article 25(1)(b)). Changing capabilities alone does not declassify the system. Capabilities and limitations must still be disclosed in the instructions for use (Article 13(3)(b)).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the Act has no moderate-risk tier and that guardrails do not alter high-risk classification, aligning with the substance of criterion 1.
The answer does not state any of the four Article 6(3) conditions for exemption; it discusses purpose narrowing and Annex III matching but omits the specific conditions listed in the criterion.
The answer confirms that changing the intended purpose can remove high-risk status if the new purpose no longer matches an Annex III use-case, which captures the substance of criterion 3.
The answer fails to mention the profiling exception in Article 6(3), which mandates high-risk status regardless of purpose or guardrails, making it silent on this key exception.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents regulatory logic in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the operator can use them. The AI Act does not ban AI-generated images of skin conditions for teaching, but if they count as a "deep fake" under Article 3(60), the deploying university must disclose that they were artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)). An image counts as a deep fake only if it resembles an existing person or thing and would falsely appear to be authentic. The lighter duty (disclosing only that such content exists, without hampering the work) applies only to "evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous" works, and the Act does not say whether educational illustration counts as "analogous". The law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter duty, and only covers uses authorised by law to fight crime, so it does not apply here.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is permitted, aligning with the criterion's 'Yes, permitted'.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) if the content qualifies as a deep fake.

The answer expresses uncertainty about whether educational use qualifies as 'analogous' to artistic/creative/fictional works and does not affirm that the lighter regime applies, thus failing to state the substance of the criterion.
The answer correctly identifies that the law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and confirms it does not apply in this context.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a way usable by a compliance professional.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No, this is not a high-risk system, and it is not prohibited either. The "policing" category in Annex III, point 6 (law enforcement) covers AI used by or on behalf of law-enforcement authorities, and a supermarket's private loss-prevention tool does not fall under it. It also uses no biometrics, so Annex III, point 1 does not apply. The prohibition on social scoring in Article 5(1)(c) is not met: the tool looks only at the current cart and checkout, not at people over a period of time, and it does not score their social behaviour or personal characteristics. It also involves no treatment in an unrelated social context (Article 5(1)(c)(i)), and an optional bag check is not unjustified or disproportionate treatment (Article 5(1)(c)(ii)). The prohibition on predicting criminal offences in Article 5(1)(d) does not apply, because the flag is not based solely on profiling or personality traits. Instead, it rests on objective, verifiable transaction anomalies and only supports a human decision by store staff.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No, this is not a high-risk system', which matches the required verdict.
The answer states that the Annex III.6 category applies only to AI used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer explicitly explains that a supermarket's private loss-prevention tool does not fall under Annex III.6 because it is not used by or on behalf of law enforcement, directly satisfying the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents a coherent regulatory analysis.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 still apply to the operator's AI system. Under Article 43(3), for products covered by Section A of Annex I, the Section 2 requirements apply to the high-risk AI system and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment. The opt-out from third-party assessment is only available if you have also applied harmonised standards, or where applicable common specifications under Article 41, that cover all of the Section 2 requirements, so the opt-out assumes you have met those requirements rather than exempting you from them.
